how-much-to-charge-to-screen-a-porch.htm.text:
Screened porch bid calculator

How much to charge to screen a porch

A published “$55 a square foot” special prices the floor. A residential screened porch is not a floor. It is wall screen that does not scale with square feet, a knee wall that may be nothing or 36 inches of framed work, an existing roof or a new one, and often a ceiling and a second door. Matching the coupon on a 12×16 enclosed porch is how a sold job becomes a two-day loss after the first wall of panels.

Open the free bid calculator

The number a square-foot special cannot see

Take a 10×12 attached screen-in under an existing roof, no knee wall, fiberglass mesh, one door. That is 32 lineal feet of wall and 256 square feet of screen — on a 120 square-foot floor. The coupon says $6,600. Raise the same shop to a 12×16 enclosed porch. The floor is 192 square feet, so the coupon says $10,560. The screen did not scale that way: 40 lineal feet, a 36-inch knee wall, a new shed roof, and often beadboard on 192 square feet the 10×12 never had.

Put pet mesh or hurricane mesh on that 12×16. Screen now costs more per square foot the fiberglass 10×12 never priced. 10-foot walls are not “the same job plus two feet.” A second door is not in the square-foot number at all.

How to price it

  1. Measure width along the house and depth out from the wall.
  2. Count screenable wall: three sides if attached, four if it wraps. Wall-screen square feet is that perimeter times the screen height after the knee wall.
  3. Add panels at your widths, knee-wall lineal feet when the job is not full-height screen, and roof or ceiling on the whole floor when you are actually building them.
  4. Price mesh (fiberglass / pet / hurricane), doors, a ceiling fan, existing-screen demo, and the permit allowance.
  5. Load the wage, add materials and mobilization, mark overhead on direct cost, then divide by one minus the target margin. The walk-away price is total cost.

The screened porch bid calculator does that arithmetic in the browser from your own hours and invoices. Starting panel widths, mesh rates, and material rates are ballpark figures to replace, not a catalog or a code table.

What this is not

This is not a building-code opinion, a permit, a construction specification, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction and a qualified professional before sending a price. The output is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

No warranty. This free article and calculator are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from their use.

Common questions

How much to charge to screen a porch?

Start from the floor, count the wall-screen square feet a square-foot special cannot see, then add knee wall, roof, ceiling, mesh, extras, and the permit. A published $55 per square foot special only sees width times depth.

Why do panels and knee wall change the price?

A 10-by-12 screen-in under an existing roof is 32 lineal feet of wall and 256 square feet of screen on a 120 square-foot floor. A 12-by-16 enclosed porch adds a knee wall, a new roof, and often a ceiling. Matching the 10-by-12 coupon is how the enclosed job loses money.

Is this a building-code calculation?

No. Panel widths, spans, and mesh rates here are common starting points on residential bids. They are not a building-code opinion, a permit, or an engineering stamp.

vs-a-flat-55-a-square-foot-special.html.text:
← Screened Porch Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $55-a-square-foot special

"$55 a square foot installed" is a price for one porch — a screen-in under an existing roof, no knee wall, one door — quoted at a porch whose square footage can look like any other porch's while the knee wall, roof, and ceiling underneath it are entirely different.

What a flat per-square-foot special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline rate, read off a yard sign, a Facebook post, or a competitor's postcard and repeated for every porch afterward. Homeowners shop it because a single number is the easiest thing to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner will ask you to match at a porch that took the crew a fraction of the time — or several times longer.

The rate behind it was usually set for one porch — a screen-in under an existing roof, no knee wall, standard fiberglass mesh — and then reused for every job afterward keyed only to floor square footage, whether or not the next porch has a knee wall to frame, a new roof to build, or a ceiling to finish.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the porch's width, depth, attachment, wall height, knee wall, roof, ceiling, mesh, panel width, doors, and extras, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It turns that into whole screen panels along the perimeter, the knee-wall, roof, and ceiling hours a flat rate never separates out, and a walk-away price for this porch, not a generic one.

What a flat $55/sf special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges every porch the same rate per square foot, so a 10×12 screen-in under an existing roof and a 12×16 enclosure with a knee wall, a new roof, and a ceiling both get quoted off the same number. Prices the knee wall, roof, ceiling, and panels each porch actually needs, so this calculator's own numbers for the two jobs above are $25.77 and $67.47 a square foot — about 2.6× apart — even though a flat special would charge both the same rate.
Has no line for a knee wall — a per-square-foot number for "screened porch" does not distinguish full-height screen from a 36-inch framed knee wall. Prices 14.0 hours and $1,120 of knee wall for the 12×16 enclosure, versus zero for the 10×12 screen-in, because knee-wall lineal feet is its own input, not folded into one per-foot rate.
Has no line for a new roof or ceiling — "existing roof" and "new framed roof with beadboard" price the same under a flat rate. Prices 6.53 hours and $2,304 of roof, plus 4.61 hours and $1,440 of ceiling, for the framed-roof job, versus zero for the existing-roof job, because roof and ceiling square feet are their own inputs.
Reasons in square feet, but screen goes up in framed panels at a fixed width — so a per-foot special has no way to show that a taller wall or a knee wall changes the panel count. Counts whole panels from the perimeter and panel width: 11 panels for the 32-foot perimeter of the 10×12 screen-in, 14 panels for the 40-foot perimeter of the 12×16 enclosure.
Gives the crew a rate to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match a cheaper porch's price. Reports what quoting that same $55/sf rate actually clears on the harder job: $10,560.00, an 8.0% margin against this calculator's $9,715.20 cost — a fraction of the 25% margin the calculator solves for at its own $12,953.61 price.

A flat per-square-foot special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a porch whose square footage looks like any other porch's but whose knee wall, roof, and ceiling are not, and nothing about a yard-sign rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $55-a-square-foot special get the price wrong?

Because it charges every screened porch the same rate per square foot, and that rate cannot tell a screen-in under an existing roof from an enclosure with a knee wall, a new roof, and a ceiling. This calculator's own numbers for a 10×12 screen-in with no knee wall and a 12×16 enclosure with a 36-inch knee wall, a new framed roof, and a beadboard ceiling come out to $25.77 and $67.47 a square foot — about 2.6x apart — even though both are the same kind of job, a screened porch.

What does a flat per-square-foot rate leave out?

The knee wall, the roof, and the ceiling. A 10×12 screen-in under an existing roof with no knee wall needs none of those — this calculator prices the walls only. A 12×16 enclosure with a 36-inch knee wall, a new framed roof, and a beadboard ceiling adds 14.0 hours and $1,120 of knee wall, 6.53 hours and $2,304 of roof, and 4.61 hours and $1,440 of ceiling — 25.1 hours and $4,864 that a per-square-foot number for “screened porch” never separates out.

Why does this calculator count screen panels instead of square feet of mesh?

Because a screened porch is built from framed panels at a fixed width, not a continuous roll charged by the square foot — a shop buys and hangs whole panels, not a fraction of one. This calculator counts panels from the perimeter and panel width: 11 panels for the 32-foot perimeter of the 10×12 screen-in, and 14 panels for the 40-foot perimeter of the 12×16 enclosure, so the bid reflects what the crew actually installs.

What happens to margin when the $55 special is quoted on the harder job?

It gets thin. A flat rate special is not priced from cost — it is a headline number set for the easy job and repeated for every job afterward. Quoting the $55-a-square-foot special on the 12×16 enclosure prices at $10,560.00, which clears only 8.0% margin against this calculator's $9,715.20 cost — a fraction of the 25% margin the calculator solves for when it prices that same job at $12,953.61.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local screened-porch prices, labor rates, or what a competitor's coupon charges. It takes the porch's width, depth, wall height, knee wall, roof, ceiling, mesh, panels, doors, and extras, plus your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-square-foot special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the next porch stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

← Screened Porch Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Buildxact

Two different shapes: Buildxact is account-based estimating and project-management software for running a construction business across trades and jobs. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this screened-porch job cost, given its panels, knee wall, and roof, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Buildxact is construction estimating and project-management software founded in Australia in 2011, with North American headquarters in Austin, Texas. It serves builders, remodelers, and contractors across trades — including carpentry, painting, roofing, and flooring — combining material takeoffs, quoting, job costing, scheduling, and client communication into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every trade on the crew. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Buildxact's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — multi-trade construction estimating and project-management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Buildxact appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Buildxact does. It does not manage takeoffs across trades, schedule crews, track job costs over time, or store any project record on a server. It takes one screened-porch job — a perimeter, wall-screen and panel count, an attached or wrap layout, a knee wall, a roof and ceiling kit, screen mesh, a door, demo of an existing screen, a permit allowance, plus loaded wage, materials, mobilization, overhead, and target margin — and turns that into the job price, the price per screened square foot, the labor-hour split between framing, panels, mesh, and extras, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and signature line. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
